view: God will teach the Prophet the Qur’an and preserve his recitation so he does not forget it.
note: Some specify Gabriel as the intermediary; al-Ṭabarī links preservation with the warning against haste in 75:16–17.

view: God gathers the Qur’an in the Prophet’s heart, preserving it there and enabling its recitation on his tongue.
note: Muqātil also qualifies this preservation by what God wills to abrogate and replace.

view: God makes the Prophet a reader by inspiring recitation, so he retains what he reads.
note: Al-Bayḍāwī offers this alongside recitation through Gabriel.

view: Gabriel delivers and teaches revelation to the previously unlettered Prophet, who recites it from memory without needing a written text.
note: Al-Zajjāj says he teaches his Companions without repetition; Elmalılı identifies Gabriel as the Trustworthy and Holy Spirit and cites 42:52.

view: God enables the Prophet to recite revelation exactly as given, without addition, omission, or distortion through forgetfulness.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes full delivery of every recited revelation.

view: The promise rests on the Prophet’s unusually strong, exact memory despite his being unlettered.
note: The sources also take this retention as a sign of prophethood.

view: The Prophet will not forget the truth that he hears.
note: Al-Rāghib’s formulation.

view: The promise concerns retention of revealed law and sūras and reinforces the duty to keep them in mind.
note: This account distinguishes the verse from the haste passage in al-Qiyāmah.

view: God’s guarantee of preservation continues as the growing Qur’an is revealed, with recitation preparing for the central promise not to forget.
note: Islāḥī assigns collection, recital, following, and explanation to God.

view: The promise may concern recitation of the sūras, with the negative giving emphatic reassurance and a warning against neglecting regular review.
note: An alternative reported by Abū Ḥayyān.

view: The verb for making someone recite means teaching and making that person a reciter; it is also glossed as keeping the Qur’an in the ear.
note: The second gloss is attributed to Tāj al-maṣādir.

view: Iqraʾ can mean learning a reading by listening so errors can be corrected; qirāʾah is recitation related to gathering letters.
note: Al-Majmaʿ likewise defines making someone recite through listening and correction.

view: Reading is the joining of letters and words in measured recitation, rather than every gathering or the utterance of a single letter.
note: Definition attributed to al-Mufradāt.

view: God’s teaching the Prophet to recite does not imply correcting a misreading: no such correction or forgetting of revelation is known.
note: This rejects the corrective-listening sense as an explanation here.

view: Gabriel repeats the revelation until the Prophet memorizes it.
note: One explanation of how the promise is fulfilled.

view: God strengthens the Prophet so that he memorizes revelation after hearing it once.
note: An alternative to repeated recitation by Gabriel.

view: The Prophet could read writing but could not write, becoming a reader through inspiration without instruction.
note: Attributed to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

view: The inspired-reader interpretation conflicts with transmitted early explanations and with the causal fāʾ.
note: Al-Ālūsī’s rejection of that interpretation.

view: The verse connects the Qur’an’s comprehensive knowledge with God making it easy to act on it.
note: A third explanation of the promise.

view: The Prophet rehearsed revelation inwardly or privately because he feared forgetting it, and the promise relieved that fear.
note: Reported from Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās; Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ transmits a similar account.

view: Fearing forgetfulness, the Prophet began repeating or moving his tongue to recite revelation before Gabriel finished; God reassured him, and reports say he thereafter forgot nothing.
note: Sources attribute this to Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, Muqātil, or Ibn ʿAbbās; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he subsequently recited exactly as Gabriel did.

view: The chain of the report from Ibn ʿAbbās about reciting before Gabriel finished includes Juwaybir, judged very weak.
note: Al-Suyūṭī’s assessment of that report.

view: The Prophet struggled to retain revelation and moved his lips while Gabriel recited, but later recited it exactly as Gabriel had.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the linked report as authentic and cites 75:16–18.

view: The Prophet’s eagerness arose from love and responsibility for each letter of revelation.
note: Quṭb explains the emotional burden behind his repetition.

view: The Prophet eagerly repeated each word and wanted the whole revelation at once; God told him not to hurry because revelation follows a wise timetable.
note: The study Qur’an also stresses that revelation is given in due time.

view: The promise recalls the commands in 20:114 and 75:16–19 not to hasten recitation while revelation arrives.
note: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mālik are cited for the connection; the verse stops haste while assuring preservation.

view: The sequence may be 87:6 first, then 75:16–19, then 20:114, all addressing haste in receiving revelation.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr argues al-Qiyāmah was revealed later; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the full order plausible.

view: God’s promise to preserve the reminder in 15:9 supports this assurance.
note: Al-Zajjāj’s supporting cross-reference.

view: For qaraʾa, compare 96:1; an imperative followed by a future first-person plural revelation promise also appears in 73:2–5.
note: A literary cross-reference.

view: Falā tansā is a declarative promise that the Prophet will not forget, rather than a prohibition.
note: Al-Naḥḥās prefers this on exegetical grounds; al-Rāzī likens it to promising clothing so someone will not be naked; Ibn ʿĀshūr says declarative form functions as a guarantee.

view: Falā tansā can be a jussive prohibition against forgetting, with the final alif retained or lengthened for the verse ending.
note: Al-Bayḍāwī compares the form al-sabīlā in 33:67; Ibn Kathīr’s version excepts abrogated recitation.

view: The final yāʾ or alif in tansā is written to match the verse endings.
note: Al-Marzūqī says an alif deleted in inflection is restored when lengthened at a pause.

view: A prohibition on forgetting is strained because forgetting lies outside a person’s control.
note: Al-Rāzī additionally says it weakens divine glad tidings, requires extra constructions, and conflicts with 75:16; al-Ālūsī rejects figurative neglect and orthographic defenses.

view: A prohibition can reasonably address avoiding the causes of forgetting, so involuntariness does not settle the grammar.
note: Al-Samīn’s reply to Makkī.

view: On a prohibitive reading, the Prophet is told not to neglect recitation and repetition.
note: This reading adds an alif to fit the verse ending.

view: The future marker sīn either strengthens the promise or marks recitation now and continuing through future revelation.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr says it confirms a coming act and signals renewal alongside an act already underway.

view: The switch to God’s first-person plural marks a direct, majestic promise to the Prophet.
note: Corpus Coranicum calls the shift iltifāt; Abdel Haleem says it heightens and dramatizes authority without requiring redaction; this is the sūra’s first explicit divine speaker and promises further revelation.

view: Recitation is attributed to God because He creates and commands the words, with Gabriel acting as His intermediary.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this a rational attribution; al-Ālūsī a metonymy.

view: The object of ‘God wills’ is omitted by ordinary Arabic usage; the exception covers whatever He chooses the Prophet to forget.
note: Bursevī describes the exception as taken from the broadest class of things recited.

view: The exception covers revelation God abrogates and causes to leave memory or recitation.
note: Some specify both recitation and ruling, others only recitation; Muqātil mentions replacement with better, Bursevī erasure from pages and hearts, and Islāḥī temporary directives whose ending God announces.

view: An abrogated verse ceases to be recited or used in prayer and eventually leaves memory.
note: Al-Rāzī attributes the first formulation to Muqātil.

view: The exception covers what God abrogates, removing both the recitation and its ruling.
note: An explicit twofold account of abrogation.

view: Abrogated recitation is forgotten because God has the Prophet and community stop reciting it.
note: Bursevī adds erasure from pages and hearts.

view: A revealed stoning verse and a warning against disowning one’s fathers are reported as examples of material once revealed.
note: Report attributed to ʿUmar in the discussion of abrogated recitation.

view: God may make the Prophet forget what He wills; reports say he forgot nothing beyond that exception.
note: Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās are among the reported speakers; Ibn ʿAbbās’s report extends the claim through the Prophet’s death.

view: The exception may permit a temporary ordinary lapse followed by recollection through a reminder.
note: Some call such lapses rare; this differs from permanent loss through abrogation.

view: The Prophet omitted a verse during prayer; Ubayy asked if it had been abrogated, and the Prophet answered that he had forgotten it.
note: Bursevī adds that the answer followed Ubayy’s question.

view: A man’s nighttime recitation reminded the Prophet of verses he had omitted or forgotten.
note: Abū Ḥayyān names the reciter ʿAbbād; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites ʿĀʾishah’s report.

view: God may make the Prophet forget something in order to establish it as a practice.
note: Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās.

view: Forgetting may be limited to a rare lapse of etiquette or sunnah, not an obligation, because losing a required ruling would damage the law.
note: A boundary on permissible lapses.

view: The Prophet is protected from forgetting what he must convey, although other temporary or purposeful forgetting is possible.
note: Al-Qushayrī allows forgetting material outside the duty to convey before it is conveyed.

view: The exception refers to a revelation God delays, so the Prophet has not yet recited it.
note: Attributed to Ibn ʿĪsā.

view: The exception is conventional or rhetorical, with no particular forgotten revelation intended; the promise denies forgetting in practice.
note: Al-Farrāʾ compares conventional exceptions in speech and oaths and 11:107; al-Kalbī says nothing was forgotten after the verse; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also sees preserved power to cause forgetting.

view: An empty exception makes God’s exception no exception at all and is unsuitable even in eloquent speech.
note: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the conventional-formula account.

view: The non-actual exception teaches saying ‘if God wills’ about a future event, even when its outcome is known.
note: Connected to 18:23–24.

view: The exception keeps the Prophet vigilant about whether any revealed portion could be excluded.
note: A proposed purpose for a non-actual exception.

view: The exception expresses God’s continuing power and free will to cause forgetting even after promising preservation, though He does not exercise it.
note: Al-Farrāʾ says preservation is God’s favor rather than the Prophet’s own power; Quṭb extends the principle to God’s lasting laws and promises.

view: The Prophet reads the universal Qur’an of realities inscribed in his preparedness and Qur’anic intellect, remembering it without forgetting.
note: Al-Qāshānī’s inward reading.

view: God may remove the Prophet’s awareness of something now and reserve it for his praiseworthy station at resurrection.
note: Al-Qāshānī’s reading of the exception.

view: Not forgetting means not neglecting or abandoning action on revelation’s commands and prohibitions.
note: Al-Junayd is repeatedly credited; al-Ālūsī reports this as a promise of compliance but rejects it as far-fetched.

view: On the practice reading, God protects the Prophet from abandoning a teaching except where God abrogates its application.
note: Al-Māwardī’s variant allows what God permits as a concession and reads the statement as prohibiting shirk.

view: Ibn Kaysān praised Junayd’s explanation that the Prophet would not forget to act on revelation and said Junayd deserved to preside.
note: Muḥammad al-Baghdādī reports Ibn Kaysān’s attendance at Junayd’s gathering and his question.

view: The practice reading is far-fetched as an interpretation of the promise.
note: Al-Ālūsī’s rejection.

view: Forgetfulness is an act created by God.
note: Abū ʿAlī’s account.

view: Forgetfulness is a loss of ordinarily necessary knowledge, rather than a distinct entity or act.
note: Abū Hāshim’s alternative to Abū ʿAlī.

view: An unlettered man retained and taught an extensive book without study, writing, or repeated rehearsal; this is a sign of prophethood.
note: Al-Rāzī stresses the book’s extent; al-Ālūsī adds the Qur’an’s inimitability and reports of unseen events; Kuran Yolu sees the sign continuing in communal memorization.

view: Because an early Meccan promise of extraordinary recitation and retention was later fulfilled, the accurate prediction is itself a further miracle.
note: Al-Rāzī emphasizes foreknowledge; al-Biqāʿī distinguishes the recitation and fulfilled prediction.

view: The Prophet’s protected memory is a proof of God’s power, also visible in the community’s ability to read and memorize the Qur’an.
note: Kuran Yolu’s extension to the community.

view: The promise follows the command to glorify because complete glorification includes reciting God’s revelation, relieving the Prophet’s fear of forgetting.
note: Abū Ḥayyān says any forgetfulness reserved by the exception serves a divine purpose.

view: The previous sūra calls revelation decisive speech, and this sūra identifies that speech with God’s promise to recite it to the Prophet.
note: Linked to 86:13.

view: The sūra moves from general guidance to creatures to special guidance of the Messenger: receiving and preserving the Qur’an and guiding humanity.
note: Al-Biqāʿī lists God’s existence, attributes, creative power, guidance, and governance as the preceding themes.

view: The sūra first establishes God’s essence, attributes, self-subsistence, and acts, leading from recognition of prophethood to obedience and countering ignorance and arrogant denial.
note: Al-Biqāʿī’s ordering of the argument.

view: The sūra affirms God’s freedom from deficiency, including haste, inability to resurrect, purposeless creation, false speech, and speech that humans can imitate.
note: Al-Biqāʿī’s account of the sūra’s purpose.

view: Sūrat al-Ṭāriq alludes generally to denials that this sūra explains in detail.
note: Al-Biqāʿī’s connection between the sūras.

view: Human flourishing requires an infallible exemplar, while love for God’s sake supports religion.
note: Al-Biqāʿī’s rationale for turning to the Messenger.

view: God repeatedly makes the unlettered Prophet a reciter, fully knowledgeable in life-giving revelation and able to spread and clarify it.
note: The Messenger’s role in the sūra’s movement.

view: Worldly ornaments and pleasures perish like withered debris; attachment to them distracts from special glorification and veils a person’s possible perfection.
note: Bursevī includes food and drink and describes glorification as stripping the divine essence of attachments.

view: The sūra steadies the Prophet with promised revelation, a gracious law, and a book that reminds the purified and God-fearing.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr’s account of the sūra’s support for the mission.

view: Revelation confirms earlier messengers’ scriptures and so comforts the Prophet amid pagan rejection.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr’s connection to earlier scriptures.

view: God’s fashioning and guidance equip the Prophet for his mission, including retention of revelation and an easy law.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr connects 87:6 and 87:8 with the sūra’s earlier themes.

view: The opening command to glorify gives general glad tidings; here God explicitly promises preservation of every recited revelation for full delivery.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr’s account of the passage’s placement.

view: The Prophet’s preservation and obedience are assured because God knows both what is manifest and his hidden concern for revelation.
note: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links the guarantee to God’s knowledge.

view: The shift to third-person ‘He knows’ points to divine power as the basis for the exception.
note: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī’s explanation of the shift.

view: God’s assurance comforts the Prophet and community because the faith originates with God, who guards it in the Prophet’s heart.
note: Quṭb’s account of the reassurance.

view: The preceding sūra tells the Prophet that persistent deniers have only temporary respite and cannot escape God; this sūra turns primarily to him to ease his preaching fears.
note: Islāḥī sees the reassurance continuing across at least ten subsequent sūras.

view: Verses 6–8 promise revelation’s maturation and preservation, with only what God sets aside excepted, and ease after known hardships.
note: Islāḥī reads the three promises together.

view: The gradual order seen in human development and vegetation also governs prophethood: revelation will mature and the Prophet will overcome obstacles.
note: Islāḥī’s analogy with earlier natural images.

view: The Prophet’s eagerness for revelation came from needing support against opposition, guidance for the future, and answers to objections.
note: Islāḥī connects this need with 20:114 and 75:16.
